```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6)
library(paweh)
```

# Why compare a child with their parents?

Suppose a clinic can recruit 600 children with a childhood disease and both
parents of each child. A nearby DNA marker has two versions, or *alleles*,
called A and a. Do affected children inherit A more often than expected from
parents who could pass on either allele? How many families would give the
study a good chance of detecting such a difference?

In an unrelated case-control study, cases and controls might come from
populations where A has different frequencies. If disease prevalence also
differs between those populations, a difference in allele frequencies can
look like a disease association. This is *population stratification*. The
transmission disequilibrium test (TDT; Spielman, McGinnis, and Ewens, 1993)
asks which allele an affected child received **within the same family**.
Both possible alleles come from the same parent, so ancestry differences
between unrelated groups do not supply the comparison. A mistaken disease
diagnosis or an incorrect genotype can still change the result.

# What does one family contribute?

A **complete trio** consists of two biological parents and their affected
child, all genotyped at the marker. At an autosomal marker a child inherits
one allele from each parent. A parent with genotype Aa is *heterozygous*:
either A or a can be passed on. A parent with genotype aa (or AA) is
*homozygous*: both copies are alike. The figure follows one of the possible
outcomes for an Aa parent and an aa parent.

```{r trio-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, fig.alt="The Aa parent transmits A and does not transmit a. The aa parent transmits a. The affected child is Aa.", fig.cap="One complete trio. Arrows trace the inherited alleles; the alternative allele is identified inside each parent's box."}
par(mar = rep(0.3, 4))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 6), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
node <- function(x, y, title, detail, fill) {
  rect(x - 2.12, y - 0.7, x + 2.12, y + 0.7,
       col = fill, border = "#334e63", lwd = 1.5)
  text(x, y + 0.22, title, font = 2)
  text(x, y - 0.28, detail, cex = 0.85)
}
node(2.4, 4.95, "Parent 1: Aa", "a was not transmitted", "#e1f2ec")
node(7.6, 4.95, "Parent 2: aa", "both copies are a", "#edf2f7")
arrows(c(2.4, 7.6), 4.18, c(4.35, 5.65), 1.78, length = 0.12,
       lwd = 2, col = c("#236752", "#334e63"))
text(2.0, 3.0, "passed A", col = "#194d3c")
text(8.0, 3.0, "passed a", col = "#334e63")
node(5, 1.0, "Affected child: Aa", "one allele from each parent", "#fff1cf")
```

Count transmissions with respect to **one prespecified allele**, here A.
Parent 1 adds one transmission of A; the untransmitted a tells us what the
child could have received instead. Had this child received a from Parent 1,
that parent would add one *non-transmission of A*. Parent 2 adds neither
count: there was no choice between A and a. A trio can thus contribute zero,
one, or two informative parental transmissions. Plan recruitment in complete
families: 600 independent trios need 1,800 people, but 1,800 individuals
alone do not guarantee even one complete trio.

# From transmissions to power

Under Mendelian segregation each heterozygous parent passes on either allele
with probability one half. Under the TDT null (no linkage or no association),
and with accurate calls and ascertainment, selecting affected children
should not systematically favor A. The observed TDT compares how often A was
transmitted with how often it was not. A sustained imbalance provides evidence
against that null; it does not establish that A itself causes disease.

Before recruiting anyone, we have no observed counts. Instead, a design model
predicts **ET**, the expected number of informative transmissions of A, and
**ENT**, the expected number of informative non-transmissions of A. These can
be fractional because they are averages over hypothetical repetitions of the
study. Deng and Chen's affected-trio calculation uses this contrast to obtain
the noncentrality parameter (NCP):

\[
\lambda = \frac{(ET-ENT)^2}{ET+ENT}.
\]

The numerator is the squared excess of one outcome over the other; either
direction counts as evidence. The denominator is the total expected number of
informative transmissions. At a given total, a larger imbalance gives a
larger NCP. At fixed transmission proportions, doubling the number of
independent families doubles the NCP. Power is the probability that the
statistic exceeds the chosen null cutoff when the modeled association is
real. The calculation uses a large-sample chi-square approximation with one
degree of freedom: central under the usual null and noncentral under the
alternative. The NCP is a design quantity, not a statistic observed in a
particular family study.

# Would 600 trios suffice?

Start with a two-allele disease locus and a marker that tags it. *Relative
risk* compares disease risk at one genotype with risk in people who carry
zero copies of the modeled disease allele. The inputs below specify an
illustrative study; the disease definition and frequencies would need
independent justification in a real design.

| Input | Value | Meaning in this design |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `N` | 600 | Complete affected-child trios available for a power calculation. |
| `pd` | 0.30 | Population frequency of the disease allele; the modeled marker allele has the same frequency. |
| `prev` | 0.05 | Fraction of the source population truly affected, before classification error. |
| `R1` | 1.5 | One-copy genotype has 1.5 times the zero-copy disease risk. |
| `R2` | 2.25 | Two-copy genotype has 2.25 times the zero-copy risk. |
| `alpha` | 0.05 | Nominal probability of rejecting a true null; sets the test cutoff. |
| `delta_prime` | 1 | Maximum positive linkage disequilibrium (LD) at these allele frequencies. |
| `misclass_rate` | 0.01 | Probability a truly unaffected child is classified as affected, in the phenotype scenario. |
| `heter_rate` | 0.10 | Fraction of families unlinked to the modeled locus, in a separate scenario. |
| `target_power` | 0.80 | Desired probability of detecting the modeled association when solving for sample size. |

Table: Assumptions and design targets for the first two calls.

Here each additional copy multiplies disease risk by 1.5, so
`R2 = R1^2`. Prevalence and genotype frequencies anchor those relative risks
to absolute disease probabilities (penetrances). The model assumes random
pairing of parental haplotypes (the alleles carried together on a chromosome)
and Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions. LD measures whether the marker and
disease alleles occur together more often than their marginal frequencies
predict. With equal frequencies at the two loci the implementation sets
\(D = D' p_d(1-p_d)\). The input `delta_prime` is this normalized positive
\(D'\), ranging from zero to one. A value of one means maximal positive
tagging for these frequencies; it is not a parent's probability of passing
on A. The canonical linked-family calculation assumes no recombination
between the two loci. It does not model negative LD or independently chosen
marker and disease allele frequencies.

Use `tdt_power()` when the family count is fixed. Reverse the question with
`tdt_mssn()`: find the minimum sample size needed (MSSN) for 80% power.
These calls return a baseline and two **separate** sensitivity scenarios.

```{r basic-tdt}
basic_tdt_power <- tdt_power(
  N = 600, input_mode = "model_based",
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  alpha = 0.05, delta_prime = 1,
  misclass_rate = 0.01, heter_rate = 0.10,
  verbose = FALSE
)

basic_tdt_mssn <- tdt_mssn(
  target_power = 0.80, input_mode = "model_based",
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  alpha = 0.05, delta_prime = 1,
  misclass_rate = 0.01, heter_rate = 0.10,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r basic-tdt-table, echo=FALSE}
required <- unlist(basic_tdt_mssn$N, use.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Baseline", "Phenotype misclassification", "Locus heterogeneity"),
  Power = unlist(basic_tdt_power$power, use.names = FALSE),
  MSSN = required, Trios = ceiling(required)
), digits = 4, caption = "Power at 600 trios and trios needed for 80% power.")
```

At 600 trios the baseline has about 99.67% power. Changing only the disease
labels lowers power to 97.51%; changing only the mix of families gives 98.79%.
Reading down the last column instead, the three plans need 215, 307, and 266
whole trios, respectively. Round sample sizes up, and budget separately for
incomplete families. Neither modified row models both mechanisms together.

# What if the expected counts are already known?

A genetic model supplies counts by predicting transmissions. Alternatively,
a pilot study or an external model may supply estimates of ET and ENT for a
known number of similar trios. The `model_free` interface uses those counts;
their relevance still depends on the marker, case definition, and recruitment
population matching the proposed study.

The next calculation makes the units visible. Define `gT` as the probability
that a randomly selected parental contribution from an affected-child trio
is informative **and** transmits A; `gNT` is the probability that it is
informative **and** does not transmit A. There are two parental contributions
per trio, so ET = 2 × number of trios × gT, and likewise for ENT. Homozygous
parents contribute to neither event. The two probabilities need not add to one
and are not case or control genotype frequencies.

Here `N_star = 500` is the design size used by the count helper. Setting
`pi = 1` puts all families in the linked group. This example retains the
helpers' default `theta1 = pd` (0.30). In the published count equations
this position represents the recombination fraction in linked families
(Chen et al., 2009, Appendix), whereas the canonical model-based example
above uses zero. Set `theta1 = 0` explicitly in all three helpers to match
that linkage assumption.

```{r expected-counts}
gT <- tdt_expected_transmission_probability(
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  delta_prime = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
gNT <- tdt_expected_nontransmission_probability(
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  delta_prime = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
expected_counts <- tdt_expected_transmission_counts(
  N_star = 500,
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  delta_prime = 1, pi = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r expected-counts-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("gT (per parent)", "gNT (per parent)", "ET (500 trios)", "ENT (500 trios)"),
  Value = c(gT$gT_star, gNT$gNT_star, expected_counts$ET_star, expected_counts$ENT_star)
), digits = 4, caption = "From parental probabilities to expected counts in 500 families.")
```

Of 1,000 parental contributions, the model expects about 246.52 informative
transmissions and 210.00 informative non-transmissions of A. The informative
fraction is about 46%; *among informative contributions*, the predicted share
transmitting A is about 54%. To compare power interfaces fairly, give both
the very same counts and cutoff:

```{r model-free-power, message=FALSE}
count_power <- tdt_power_from_expected_counts(
  ET = expected_counts$ET_star,
  ENT = expected_counts$ENT_star,
  alpha = 0.05
)

canonical_model_free <- tdt_power(
  N = 500, input_mode = "model_free",
  ET = expected_counts$ET_star,
  ENT = expected_counts$ENT_star,
  misclass_rate = 0, heter_rate = 0,
  verbose = FALSE
)

c(lower_level_power = count_power[["Power"]],
  canonical_power = canonical_model_free$power$no_error)
```

Both calls give about 40.12% power (NCP 2.92): in repeated studies under
these assumptions, roughly four in ten would detect the imbalance. This
agreement checks the count-to-power calculation, not equivalence to the
earlier 600-family genetic model. For fixed-sample power, `N` must equal
the number of trios represented by the **absolute** counts. For model-free
MSSN, give that source count as `n_trios`, so the function can infer rates
per parent before solving for a *new* family count. For a nonzero modifier
supply `pd` where possible; the implementation can infer it only under its
allele-frequency assumptions. Phenotype misclassification also needs `prev`.

# Misread genotypes: the model in Gordon, Finch, and Kim (2020)

A laboratory might report Aa as AA. That can hide an informative parent,
create an apparent transmission, or produce a child whose called genotype is
impossible given the parents' calls. This is an error in the measured DNA
genotype, a different problem from assigning the wrong disease diagnosis.
Gordon, Finch, and Kim's *Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics*, Chapter 5,
*Designing Genetic Linkage and Association Studies that Maintain Desired
Statistical Power in the Presence of Mixtures*, treats this problem in
§5.2.5 (pp. 277–284). Its one-parameter illustration adapts the error model of
Douglas, Skol, and Boehnke (2002).

Code a genotype by its number of A copies: aa = 0, Aa = 1, AA = 2. An
*adjacent* error changes the called count by one copy. The parameter
`genotype_misclassification_rate`, denoted by \(e\), is the probability of
**each allowed change**, with \(0 \le e \le 0.5\). Read across a row for
one person's possible laboratory calls:

| True copies | Called 0 | Called 1 | Called 2 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 (aa) | \(1-e\) | \(e\) | 0 |
| 1 (Aa) | \(e\) | \(1-2e\) | \(e\) |
| 2 (AA) | 0 | \(e\) | \(1-e\) |

Table: Transition matrix from true to called marker genotype (textbook Eq. 5.19).

At \(e=0.01\), aa is called Aa 1% of the time and never AA. An Aa genotype
has two possible wrong calls, each with probability 1%, so its total error
probability is 2%. An AA genotype can be called Aa but never aa. The model
applies these probabilities independently to both parents and the child.

Suppose both parents are called aa but the child is called Aa. No parental
call can supply A, so this implementation excludes the called trio as
*Mendelian-inconsistent*. Of 27 possible ordered call patterns, 15 are
consistent. Removing the other patterns leaves less than unit probability;
dividing each retained probability by their sum gives the distribution
**among families that pass the check**. A consistent call can still be
wrong. The function counts informative transmissions in this conditional
distribution (§5.2.5.1, Eqs. 5.21–5.22).

Use the original 600-family design again, now changing only the genotype
calls. The last column rounds up the required number of analyzable trios.

```{r genotype-misclassification}
genotype_error_power <- tdt_power(
  N = 600, input_mode = "model_based",
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  alpha = 0.05, delta_prime = 1,
  effect = "genotype_misclassification",
  genotype_misclassification_rate = 0.01,
  verbose = FALSE
)

genotype_error_mssn <- tdt_mssn(
  target_power = 0.80, input_mode = "model_based",
  pd = 0.30, prev = 0.05, R1 = 1.5, R2 = 2.25,
  alpha = 0.05, delta_prime = 1,
  effect = "genotype_misclassification",
  genotype_misclassification_rate = 0.01,
  verbose = FALSE
)

genotype_error_mssn_values <- c(
  genotype_error_mssn$N$no_error,
  genotype_error_mssn$N$genotype_misclassification
)
```

```{r genotype-misclassification-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Accurate calls", "1% per adjacent error"),
  Power = c(genotype_error_power$power$no_error,
            genotype_error_power$power$genotype_misclassification),
  MSSN = genotype_error_mssn_values, Trios = ceiling(genotype_error_mssn_values)
), digits = 4, caption = "Power at 600 retained trios and retained trios needed for 80% nominal power.")
```

At 600 analyzable trios, the expected counts move from 328.70 versus 219.13
to 324.95 versus 223.04. Their smaller contrast lowers the NCP from 21.91 to
18.95. Power falls from 99.67% to 99.17%, and 80% nominal power now
requires **249 rather than 215 retained trios**. About 98.63% of called
families pass the consistency check in the error scenario. Recruiting exactly
249 families therefore does not guarantee 249 usable trios.

There is a second cost: at the nominal 5% cutoff, the modeled null rejection
rate at 600 trios is about **5.75%**
(`genotype_error_power$genotype_misclassification$actual_alpha`).
Neither the power nor the sample-size result recalibrates that cutoff. The
book demonstrates null rejection-rate inflation; the 600-family power
comparison is a package illustration under a disease alternative, not a
published power benchmark or a correction for errors in observed data.

# Children classified as affected: Buyske et al. (2009)

Suppose screening captures all children with the disease, but also labels 5%
of unaffected children as affected. With 1% prevalence, among 10,000
children we would expect 100 true cases and about 495 false positives
(5% of 9,900). Only about one in six screen-positive children would be a
true case. This is why `misclass_rate = 0.05` does **not** mean that 5% of
enrolled trios have a wrong diagnosis: the rate is conditional on being
unaffected. The added families dilute the disease-related transmission
contrast.

Buyske et al. studied this one-way error for a multiplicative risk model.
Use their stringent cutoff of 0.00001, 80% power, equal allele frequencies
of 0.50, maximal positive LD and a two-copy relative risk of 2.5. The table
compares their published example (p. 291) with this calculation. Compute the
package ratio from the unrounded estimates.

```{r buyske-reproduction}
buyske <- tdt_mssn(
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.50, prev = 0.01,
  R1 = sqrt(2.5), R2 = 2.5,
  delta_prime = 1,
  misclass_rate = 0.05, heter_rate = 0,
  verbose = FALSE
)

buyske_ratio <- buyske$N$misclassification / buyske$N$no_error
```

```{r buyske-reproduction-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Baseline trios", "Trios with false positives", "Final / baseline"),
  Published = c(691, 27118, 27118 / 691),
  paweh = c(ceiling(buyske$N$no_error), ceiling(buyske$N$misclassification),
            buyske_ratio)
), digits = 2, caption = "Buyske et al. and paweh: whole trios and the final-to-baseline ratio.")
```

The package needs **546 versus 21,401** whole trios. A ratio of 39.23 means
the final study needs about 39 times as many trios; the **increase** is
\(100(39.22715-1)\), about **3,822.7%**. The paper reports **691 versus
27,118**, also about 39-fold. The *relative* result is reproduced, not the
absolute sample sizes. Gordon, Finch, and Kim (§5.2.6, p. 285) identify a
missing factor in the paper's Eq. 5 and give corrected transmission
equations. This does not, by itself, establish the reason for the difference
in the no-error counts.

## How much does case definition matter?

For a clinic that cannot know its false-positive rate exactly, vary that rate
while holding prevalence and all other design assumptions fixed. Each point
is a separate sample-size calculation.

```{r buyske-curve, fig.cap="Required affected-child trios as phenotype misclassification increases under the Buyske model."}
plot_tdt_mssn(
  x_var = "misclass_rate",
  x_values = seq(0, 0.05, by = 0.005),
  scenario = "misclassification",
  input_mode = "model_based",
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.50, prev = 0.01,
  R1 = sqrt(2.5), R2 = 2.5,
  delta_prime = 1, heter_rate = 0,
  title = "Required trios vs phenotype misclassification"
)
```

A steeper segment means that the same extra percentage point of
false-positive classifications costs more families. Here tightening the
case definition near the high-error end could save thousands of trios, if
the other assumptions hold. The curve is a sensitivity analysis, not an
uncertainty interval.

To explore prevalence as well, run the optional Plotly code in an interactive
session. The height at each pair of coordinates is the required trio count.
The widget is omitted from the installed article to keep its size small.

```{r buyske-surface, eval=FALSE}
plot_tdt_surface3d(
  metric = "mssn", scenario = "misclassification",
  x = "prev", y = "misclass_rate",
  x_values = c(0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04),
  y_values = seq(0, 0.05, length.out = 5),
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.50, R1 = sqrt(2.5), R2 = 2.5,
  delta_prime = 1, heter_rate = 0
)
```

Compare points at the same error rate: a smaller underlying pool of true
cases makes the same false-positive rate more costly. The grid varies study
assumptions; its heights are not probabilities that those assumptions hold.

# One clinical diagnosis, several genetic causes: Chen et al. (2009)

Two children can meet the same disease definition for different genetic
reasons. If the marker tracks a disease locus in some families but is
unlinked to the cause in others, even perfectly diagnosed families can dilute
the signal. Chen et al. model a *linked fraction*, called `pi` in the count
helper, and an *unlinked fraction*, `heter_rate = 1 - pi` in the canonical
functions. In the unlinked component the recombination fraction is one half:
the marker and disease locus segregate independently, giving no systematic
excess of transmissions over non-transmissions. The mixture fraction
describes **families**, not the proportion of children misdiagnosed or the
population frequency of an allele.

Recreate the comparison in Chen et al., Figure 2: use 80% power at 0.00001,
allele frequencies of 0.25, prevalence of 0.10 and a multiplicative model
with two-copy relative risk 1.5. Only the unlinked fraction changes.

```{r chen-reproduction}
chen_no_heterogeneity <- tdt_mssn(
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.25, prev = 0.10,
  R1 = sqrt(1.5), R2 = 1.5,
  delta_prime = 1,
  misclass_rate = 0, heter_rate = 0,
  verbose = FALSE
)

chen_half_heterogeneous <- tdt_mssn(
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.25, prev = 0.10,
  R1 = sqrt(1.5), R2 = 1.5,
  delta_prime = 1,
  misclass_rate = 0, heter_rate = 0.50,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r chen-reproduction-table, echo=FALSE}
required <- c(chen_no_heterogeneity$N$heterogeneity,
              chen_half_heterogeneous$N$heterogeneity)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Unlinked = c("0%", "50%"), Published = c(3430, 13721),
  MSSN = required, Trios = ceiling(required)
), digits = 2, caption = "Chen et al., Figure 2: published trios and paweh estimates.")
```

Chen et al. report 3,430 trios for a homogeneous sample and 13,721 with
half the families unlinked. The corresponding package requirements rounded
up are **3,431 and 13,723 trios**. Both give essentially a fourfold increase
in the final study size. Half as many signal-carrying families per recruited
trio means roughly half the transmission contrast; the contrast enters the
NCP *squared*. The paper does not establish an exact reason for the small
absolute differences.

To plan between those endpoints, vary only the unlinked fraction; each point
below solves again for the same target power.

```{r chen-curve, fig.cap="Required affected-child trios as the heterogeneous or unlinked fraction increases under the Chen model."}
plot_tdt_mssn(
  x_var = "heter_rate",
  x_values = seq(0, 0.50, by = 0.05),
  scenario = "heterogeneity",
  input_mode = "model_based",
  target_power = 0.80, alpha = 1e-5,
  pd = 0.25, prev = 0.10,
  R1 = sqrt(1.5), R2 = 1.5,
  delta_prime = 1, misclass_rate = 0,
  title = "Required trios vs locus heterogeneity"
)
```

Moving right means recruiting from a less genetically homogeneous population
while keeping the disease definition unchanged. The rising slope shows that
each additional five percentage points of unlinked families costs more trios
near 50% than near zero. A pilot estimate of the linked fraction can help
decide which part of this curve to budget for.

# Choosing a TDT design

Begin with the constraint your study actually faces, then choose the
assumptions supported by your evidence.

| Question or evidence | Choice |
|:---|:---|
| We can obtain a fixed number of complete trios. | Use `tdt_power(N = ...)`; read power at that number of families. |
| We need a specified probability of detection. | Use `tdt_mssn(target_power = ...)`; round up and allow for losses separately. |
| We know prevalence, allele frequency and plausible genotype risks. | Use `input_mode = "model_based"` and state the assumed positive LD. |
| An earlier population supplies expected informative counts. | Use `"model_free"` with ET, ENT and the number of trios that produced them. |
| Screening may admit unaffected children. | Vary `misclass_rate`; specify the true prevalence, even with count inputs. |
| Correctly diagnosed families may be unlinked to this locus. | Vary `heter_rate` over a plausible range, with the linked fraction equal to one minus that rate. |
| DNA calls may be wrong by one allele copy. | Use `effect = "genotype_misclassification"` with model-based input and the scalar adjacent-error rate. Inspect retention and actual alpha as well as power. |

Table: Match the study constraint, available information and source of error to a design calculation.

For a single comparison, select `effect = "none"`,
`"phenotype_misclassification"`, `"locus_heterogeneity"`, or
`"genotype_misclassification"`. Supplying both phenotype and heterogeneity
rates in the default interface returns separate scenarios. There is no joint
model for these mechanisms; genotype misclassification cannot be layered
onto either, inferred from ET and ENT alone, or specified by a custom
transition matrix. The adjacent-call model does not describe sequencing
reads or read depth. These functions plan studies; they do not perform
TDTae, the error-aware association test for observed family data.

# Methods and references

The family diagram and the first two worked designs illustrate the original
TDT and its prospective power calculation. The genotype example extends
the textbook's null-error calculation; the Buyske and Chen sections compare
published designs with package results. The sensitivity curves and surface
are package extensions of those scenarios.

- Spielman RS, McGinnis RE, Ewens WJ (1993). Transmission test for linkage
  disequilibrium: the insulin gene region and insulin-dependent diabetes
  mellitus (IDDM). *American Journal of Human Genetics* 52:506–516.
  PMID: 8447318. Original within-family test.
- Deng HW, Chen WM (2001). The power of the transmission disequilibrium
  test (TDT) with both case-parent and control-parent trios. *Genetical
  Research* 78:289–302. <https://doi.org/10.1017/S001667230100533X>.
  The affected-child component underlies the expected-count NCP used here.
- Douglas JA, Skol AD, Boehnke M (2002). Probability of detection of
  genotyping errors and mutations as inheritance inconsistencies in
  nuclear-family data. *American Journal of Human Genetics* 70:487–495.
  <https://doi.org/10.1086/338919>. Antecedent of the textbook error model.
- Buyske S, Yang G, Matise TC, Gordon D (2009). When a case is not a case:
  effects of phenotype misclassification on power and sample size
  requirements for the transmission disequilibrium test with affected child
  trios. *Human Heredity* 67:287–292. <https://doi.org/10.1159/000194981>.
- Chen C, Yang G, Buyske S, Matise T, Finch SJ, Gordon D (2009).
  Transmission disequilibrium test power and sample size in the presence of
  locus heterogeneity. *Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular
  Biology* 8:Article 44. <https://doi.org/10.2202/1544-6115.1501>.
- Gordon D, Finch SJ, Kim W (2020). *Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics:
  How to Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies*.
  Springer. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-61121-7>. Chapter 1,
  §1.6.1.3 defines the statistic and §1.6.1.4 gives the design NCP
  (Eq. 1.25); Chapter 5, §§5.2.5, 5.2.6 and 5.3.3 cover genotype errors,
  phenotype errors and locus heterogeneity, respectively.
